key.explanation: Nineteen of thirty never reached first value, and seven were lost with a single relationship. Both are addressable, and both are larger than price — a discount would spend money on the cause behind four departures.

Read at equal age, retention has fallen from 47% to 28% across four consecutive cohorts. The aggregate is flat only because the newest and weakest cohorts are also the largest, which is exactly what a blended figure conceals.
The operating layer must preserve the evidence accumulated from validation, activation, retention, and economics. Constraint-led prioritisation connects them.
A conversion rate is only as trustworthy as the traffic that produced it. Incentivised or socially connected visitors create a contaminated signal.
The course builds from evidence of demand into trustworthy learning, system diagnosis, customer value, economics, and finally an operating cadence.
High complexity, risk, contract value, and stakeholder count favour a sales-led motion. Product can still assist evaluation and adoption.
Lean validation tests whether demand is actually present before costly building or campaigning. The test and its decision threshold matter more than collecting agreeable opinions.
A stage should represent a real change in buyer commitment or qualification. Otherwise pipeline math cannot locate the constraint.
A backlog is a decision and execution system. Ideas without hypothesis, metric, owner, score, status, and decision logic remain a wish list.
Early-stage growth is discovery under uncertainty. Scale-stage systems assume validated motions and optimize repeatability and throughput.
Funnel math identifies the bottleneck. Pouring more users into a broken activation step scales waste rather than growth.
A Type II error fails to reject a false null: a real effect is missed, often because the signal or sample is too weak.
₹16 lakh ÷ ₹20 lakh = 80% NRR. New-customer growth must not be smuggled into the existing cohort's performance.
B2B retention often lives at account/team and decision-maker level; B2C retention usually follows an individual buyer or repeat-use unit.
Target-customer commitments expose real trade-offs and therefore dominate passive or hypothetical signals.
The commitment spectrum gets stronger as the prospect gives up something real—money, time, reputation, or access. A pre-order dominates praise, likes, and opens.
Referral is an acquisition mechanism. Network effects change product value with network participation; an invite can occur without that value change.
The split protects the proven engine while reserving capacity for adjacent and exploratory learning. Evidence can justify later reallocation.

Channel-market fit asks whether this channel matches your product, your ICP and — the filter that gets skipped — your price point. A channel with a high cost per acquired customer cannot serve a low average contract value however good the targeting is; the arithmetic decides before the creative does.

All four parts of the decision rule are written before the experiment goes active: the metric, the scale threshold, the kill threshold, and a time or sample bound. Once the numbers are agreed in advance, the arriving data settles the question, because the argument happened while nobody knew the answer.
A/B testing earns statistical significance only after the planned sample is reached, using the baseline, minimum detectable effect and alpha fixed before either variant's result is visible.
The AHA moment is the first countable event where the product's promised value actually happens, and time to AHA is the elapsed path from first use to that event that onboarding should compress.
A 90-day growth roadmap turns the experiment backlog into twelve weeks of active work, capacity, decision dates and dependencies, with each date committed before the quarter begins.

The scaling threshold is a payback period below twelve months for a typical funded company: acquisition cash returns as gross profit within a year and can be recycled before growth consumes more capital than it returns.

rubric.label: Governing ideas
rubric.description: Replaces the single enthusiasm score with a scoring approach separating impact, evidence quality and effort, identifies the seven-day onboarding completion as the habit the product should be built around, names the undefined handoff as the pipeline leak, and treats direct customer contact as primary evidence rather than anecdote.

rubric.label: Use of the numbers
rubric.description: Cites specific figures — six slots against forty ideas, eight weeks and two prospects for the API against two weeks and nineteen recorded abandonments, the three-times renewal for onboarding inside seven days against 41% achieving it, or 210 leads against 96 accepted with six days to first contact.

rubric.label: How the ideas connect
rubric.description: Connects them: a single enthusiasm score cannot separate a visible idea from an effective one, which is why the eight-week item with no evidence outranks a two-week item with recorded behaviour behind it and a known effect on renewal.

rubric.label: The decision
rubric.description: States that the API should not take a slot this quarter on the evidence available, names the onboarding change and the handoff repair as the first two, and requires churned-customer interviews to run rather than be deferred.

rubric.label: What would change it
rubric.description: Names what would earn the API a slot — evidence tying it to retention or to a named deal — or states the organisational cost of overruling the chief executive and of holding a visible commitment.

key.explanation: Six slots and forty ideas

rubric.label: Governing ideas
rubric.description: Distinguishes demand for the product from demand for a discount, reads retention and payback by cohort rather than on blended contribution, identifies the absence of any tier above the single plan as the structural gap, and scores the backlog on evidence and effort rather than on preference.

rubric.label: Use of the numbers
rubric.description: Cites specific figures — 58% versus 21% month-three cancellation, 4% accepting the renewal price, ₹430 against ₹180 monthly contribution, ₹1,900 acquisition cost, or 340 emailed requests against nine weeks for an unrequested redesign.

rubric.label: How the ideas connect
rubric.description: Connects them: the discount bought people whose willingness to pay was never tested, so they leave before repaying a ₹1,900 acquisition cost, and permanence would convert a temporary distortion into the business's whole economics.

rubric.label: The decision
rubric.description: States that the discount should not be made permanent, names the twin-bag tier as the strongest of the three by evidence and effort, and defers the packaging redesign.

rubric.label: What would change it
rubric.description: Names what would justify a standing discount — a discounted cohort repaying acquisition cost, or the tier lifting average contribution — or states the short-term signup fall that ending it will cause.

key.explanation: The discount that paid for itself
